The Pauraque Nyctidromus albicollis, a widespread neotropical nightjar, exhibits life-history traits shaped by its energetically conservative, ground-nesting ecology. Newly hatched chicks, which emerge from eggs incubated for approximately 19.5 days [ab = approximately 19.5 days] at a nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], are covered in cryptic down and are surprisingly heavy for their developmental stage. Field measurements indicate that a typical neonate has a wet weight of around 5.5 grams [Wwb = around 5.5 grams] at hatching, a relatively robust mass that provides critical thermal inertia during the vulnerable first days of life when the altricial nestling is brooded almost continuously by the attending adult. The initial egg from which this chick hatches, prior to the onset of significant embryonic development, has a recorded wet weight of 7.2 grams [Ww0 = 7.2 grams], a figure that reflects the substantial investment of yolk and albumen required to sustain the embryo through the lengthy incubation period. This initial mass is notably higher than the birth weight itself, underscoring the metabolic costs of development inside the shell, where the embryo consumes a portion of the yolk reserves to build its tissues and fuel its physiological differentiation.

As the nestling progresses through the rapid growth phase typical of caprimulgids, it reaches a critical developmental milestone: fledging. Under the relatively stable thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of this species, measured at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the young Pauraque typically achieves its first flight at 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching]. This timing is relatively brief compared to many other bird groups of similar adult mass, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes a swift departure from the vulnerable ground nest. Following fledging, the juvenile enters a period of continued growth and somatic development, during which the body mass increases dramatically toward the ultimate adult values. The progression toward sexual maturation is a more protracted affair; while the juvenile may appear fully grown externally, the attainment of puberty is not achieved until approximately 60 days after hatching [tp = approximately 60 days after hatching] at the same metabolic temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This delay between fledging and reproductive maturity allows the young bird to refine its foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body condition before attempting to breed.

The adult body masses of Nyctidromus albicollis display a notable sexual dimorphism, with females typically being slightly lighter than their male counterparts. The ultimate wet weight for females in a healthy, free-ranging population has been documented at 52.5 grams [Wwi = 52.5 grams], whereas males, who are often more active in defending territories and engaging in aerial displays, reach a slightly higher asymptotic mass of 53.6 grams [Wwi = 53.6 grams]. This modest size difference is consistent with patterns seen in other nightjars where males are slightly larger, potentially aiding in competitive interactions and mate attraction. The basal metabolic rate, a key physiological parameter reflecting the cost of living, has been measured in captive individuals at a thermoneutral body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. The recorded resting metabolic rate reached a maximum of 83 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 83 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that places this species within the expected range for a caprimulgid of its adult body mass and underscores its energy-conserving lifestyle as an aerial insectivore that spends much of the day roosting motionless at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C].

Reproduction in the Pauraque is characterized by a remarkably conservative strategy that minimizes the energetic burden on the breeding adults. The species is strictly single-brooded, with females laying only one clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = one clutch of eggs per year] during the breeding season, which is timed to coincide with peak insect abundance in its tropical and subtropical range. Each of these clutches consists of just two eggs [N_R_i = Each of these clutches consists of just two eggs], a small number that reflects the high per-offspring investment required for a ground-nesting bird whose eggs are vulnerable to predation and whose chicks are relatively well-developed at hatching. This annual output is further constrained by the slow pace of the life cycle; the time since birth at which a female initiates her first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], typically at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during the active incubation sessions. This delayed onset of first reproduction, combined with the small clutch size and single annual brood, results in a very low annual reproductive output, a strategy that is sustainable only because of the correspondingly low adult mortality rates and relatively long lifespan.

Longevity data for Nyctidromus albicollis, derived from mark-recapture studies in long-term monitoring programs, indicate that the maximum documented lifespan in the wild is approximately 10.5 years [am = approximately 10.5 years], sustained at an active metabolic temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This longevity is remarkably high for a bird of its modest body size; for instance, many passerines of similar mass live only two to three years. This extended lifespan, likely a consequence of its secretive, nocturnal lifestyle that reduces predation risk, allows the Pauraque to compensate for its exceedingly low annual reproductive rate through multiple breeding seasons. Each year, the same female produces only a single clutch of two eggs [N_R_i = single clutch of two eggs] in one annual nesting attempt [F_R_i = one annual nesting attempt], yet over a potential decade of life, she may contribute a modest but consistent number of offspring to the population. This slow life-history pace is a classic example of a bet-hedging strategy, where the species trades high immediate reproductive output for high adult survival and a prolonged window of opportunity for reproduction across many years.
